name: Architectural Patterns

beginner.content:
What is Layered Architecture?

Layered Architecture (also called n-tier architecture) organizes an application into horizontal layers, where each layer has a specific responsibility and depends only on the layer directly beneath it.

The Classic 3-Tier Layout

+-------------------------------------+
|      Presentation Layer              |  <- Controllers, REST endpoints, UI
+-------------------------------------+
|      Business Layer                  |  <- Services, business rules
+-------------------------------------+
|      Persistence Layer               |  <- Repositories, DAOs
+-------------------------------------+
|      Database Layer                  |  <- Actual data storage
+-------------------------------------+
• Each layer only talks to the layer directly below it (strict layering) - or optionally to any layer below (relaxed layering).
• A typical Spring Boot project maps this almost 1:1: @RestController -> @Service -> @Repository -> Database.

expert.content:
Pros, Cons, and When Layering Breaks Down

Pros: simple to understand, easy to onboard new developers, clear separation of concerns, layers are individually testable/replaceable.
Cons: can encourage an "anemic" design where business logic leaks into controllers; a change to one layer can still ripple through several layers (the "sinkhole" anti-pattern, where a request just passes straight through every layer doing nothing); doesn't inherently protect the domain model from infrastructure concerns (that's what Hexagonal/Clean/Onion architecture add on top).

Strict vs Relaxed Layering

• Strict: a layer may ONLY call the layer immediately below it.
• Relaxed: a layer may call any layer below it (e.g. Presentation calling Persistence directly for a simple read) - more flexible but easier to turn into a tangled mess if undisciplined.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the "sinkhole" anti-pattern?A request passes through most layers doing nothing meaningful, adding overhead without real value - a sign the layering is too rigid for that use case
Strict vs relaxed layering?Strict allows a layer to call only the one directly below it; relaxed allows calling any layer below, trading discipline for flexibility
How does Spring Boot map to layered architecture?@RestController (presentation) -> @Service (business) -> @Repository (persistence) -> database

beginner.content:
What is Hexagonal Architecture?

Also called Ports & Adapters, this style puts the core business logic at the center, completely isolated from external concerns (database, UI, messaging, third-party APIs). The core defines ports (interfaces) describing what it needs; adapters implement those ports to plug in a specific technology.

        REST Adapter          JDBC Adapter
              \                    /
               \                  /
          [ Port: In ]     [ Port: Out ]
                \               /
                 \             /
              +-----------------+
              |   CORE DOMAIN   |
              |  (business logic)|
              +-----------------+
                 /             \
          [ Port: In ]     [ Port: Out ]
               /                  \
        CLI Adapter          Kafka Adapter
• Inbound ports - how the outside world drives the application (e.g. a PlaceOrderUseCase interface).
• Outbound ports - what the application needs from the outside world (e.g. an OrderRepository interface the core defines, but doesn't implement).
• Swapping the database or the UI technology never touches the core - you only write a new adapter.

expert.content:
Testability — the Biggest Practical Win

Because the core only depends on interfaces (ports), you can unit-test all business logic with a simple in-memory fake implementing OrderRepositoryPort - no database, no Spring context, no test containers needed for core logic tests. Only adapter-level tests need the real infrastructure.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's a "port" in Hexagonal Architecture?An interface the core domain defines to describe what it needs (outbound) or offers (inbound), without knowing which technology implements it
What's an "adapter"?A concrete implementation of a port that connects the core to a specific technology (a REST controller, a JPA repository, a Kafka consumer)
Why does this improve testability?Business logic can be unit tested against fake/in-memory port implementations, with zero dependency on real infrastructure

beginner.content:
What is Clean Architecture?

Popularized by Robert C. Martin ("Uncle Baji"), Clean Architecture arranges the system as concentric circles, with a single, strict rule: The Dependency Rule - source code dependencies can only point inward. Nothing in an inner circle can know anything about an outer circle.

   +-------------------------------------------+
   |     Frameworks & Drivers (DB, Web, UI)     |
   |   +-------------------------------------+   |
   |   |     Interface Adapters              |   |
   |   |   +-------------------------------+   |   |
   |   |   |   Application Business Rules  |   |   |  <- Use Cases
   |   |   |   +----------------------+   |   |   |
   |   |   |   | Enterprise Business  |   |   |   |  <- Entities
   |   |   |   |       Rules          |   |   |   |
   |   |   |   +----------------------+   |   |   |
   |   |   +-------------------------------+   |   |
   |   +-------------------------------------+   |
   +-------------------------------------------+
• Entities (innermost) - core business objects/rules, framework-independent.
• Use Cases - application-specific business rules, orchestrate entities.
• Interface Adapters - controllers, presenters, gateways - convert data between use cases and the outside world.
• Frameworks & Drivers (outermost) - Spring, the database, the web framework - the most volatile, most replaceable layer.

expert.content:
Clean vs Hexagonal vs Onion — What's Actually Different?

AspectHexagonalCleanOnion
VisualizationHexagon with ports on each side4 concentric circlesConcentric rings (domain center)
Core ideaIsolate core via ports/adaptersStrict inward-only dependency rule across explicit layersDomain model at center, infrastructure at edges
Practical differenceAll three achieve essentially the same goal (dependency inversion protecting business logic from infrastructure) - the differences are largely in emphasis and vocabulary, not substance

In practice, most real Spring Boot projects blend ideas from all three rather than rigidly following one.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is "The Dependency Rule"?Source code dependencies can only point inward - an inner circle must never reference anything in an outer circle
Which circle is most volatile/replaceable?The outermost (Frameworks & Drivers) - swapping the web framework or DB technology shouldn't touch the Entities or Use Cases
Are Clean, Hexagonal, and Onion fundamentally different?No - they share the same core goal (protect business logic from infrastructure via dependency inversion), differing mainly in visualization and terminology

beginner.content:
What is Onion Architecture?

Coined by Jeffrey Palermo, Onion Architecture puts the domain model at the absolute center, with concentric rings of increasingly infrastructure-focused code around it - like the layers of an onion. All dependencies point toward the center.

   +-----------------------------------------+
   |   Infrastructure (DB, UI, external APIs) |
   |   +-----------------------------------+   |
   |   |   Application Services            |   |
   |   |   +-----------------------------+   |   |
   |   |   |   Domain Services           |   |   |
   |   |   |   +----------------------+  |   |   |
   |   |   |   |  Domain Model /      |  |   |   |
   |   |   |   |  Entities (center)   |  |   |   |
   |   |   |   +----------------------+  |   |   |
   |   |   +-----------------------------+   |   |
   |   +-----------------------------------+   |
   +-----------------------------------------+
• The domain model at the very center has zero dependencies on anything else in the system.
• Infrastructure concerns (persistence, UI frameworks) are pushed to the outermost ring, exactly where they belong given how often they change.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What sits at the absolute center of Onion Architecture?The domain model / entities, with zero dependencies on anything outside
Where does infrastructure code live?The outermost ring, since it's the most likely to change (swap databases, UI frameworks, etc.)

beginner.content:
What is Microservices Architecture?

An architectural style that structures an application as a collection of small, independently deployable services, each built around a specific business capability, each owning its own data store, and communicating over the network (typically HTTP/REST or messaging).

  [Order Service] --- owns ---> [Order DB]
  [Payment Service] --- owns ---> [Payment DB]
  [Inventory Service] --- owns ---> [Inventory DB]
        \           |            /
         \          |           /
          [ API Gateway / Load Balancer ]
                     |
                  Clients
• Each service can be developed, deployed, and scaled independently.
• Different services can even use different tech stacks (polyglot).

expert.content:
Tradeoffs vs a Monolith

AspectMonolithMicroservices
DeploymentOne unit, all-or-nothingIndependent per service
ScalingScale the whole appScale only the hot service
Data consistencyEasy - one DB, real transactionsHard - needs Saga/eventual consistency
Operational complexityLowHigh (service discovery, distributed tracing, network failures)
Team autonomyCoordination-heavyTeams can own/deploy services independently

Microservices trade simplicity for independent scalability and team autonomy - they are NOT free, and are usually not the right first choice for a small team or an early-stage product.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the single biggest operational cost of microservices?Distributed systems complexity - network failures, eventual consistency, service discovery, distributed tracing/debugging
Should a startup begin with microservices?Usually no - starting with a well-modularized monolith and splitting out services only when there's a proven scaling/team need is the more common, safer path

beginner.content:
What is a Monolithic Architecture?

A monolith is an application built and deployed as a single, unified unit - one codebase, one build, one deployment artifact (e.g. one Spring Boot JAR/WAR), even if internally it's organized into modules/packages.

• Why it's still often the right choice: simplest to develop, test, deploy, and debug; no network calls between "modules"; real ACID transactions across the whole domain; lowest operational overhead.
• When it becomes a problem: the codebase grows large enough that any change requires understanding too much of the system; different parts need to scale very differently; many teams stepping on each other in one codebase/deployment pipeline.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Is a monolith automatically "bad" architecture?No - it's often the pragmatic, correct starting point; the "distributed monolith" (microservices with monolith-level coupling but network overhead) is worse than either extreme
What signals it's time to consider splitting a monolith?Distinct parts needing very different scaling, deployment cadence, or team ownership boundaries that the monolith is actively getting in the way of

beginner.content:
What is a Modular Monolith?

A middle ground between a tangled monolith and microservices: still one deployable unit, but internally organized into strongly-bounded modules with explicit interfaces between them - each module could, in principle, become its own microservice later with minimal rework.

+------------------- One Deployable JAR -------------------+
|  [Orders module]   [Payments module]   [Inventory module] |
|   only talks to        only talks to      only talks to   |
|   Payments via a        Orders via a       Orders via a    |
|   defined interface     defined interface  defined interface |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
• Modules communicate only through explicit, well-defined interfaces - never by reaching into another module's internal classes/tables directly.
• Gives most of a monolith's simplicity today, with a much cheaper migration path to microservices later if it's ever actually needed.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How does a modular monolith differ from a plain monolith?It enforces strict module boundaries and explicit interfaces between modules, rather than allowing any class to reach into any other part of the codebase
Why is it an easier migration path to microservices?Because module boundaries are already well-defined, extracting a module into its own service mainly means replacing an in-process call with a network call, not redesigning the boundary

beginner.content:
What is Event-Driven Architecture?

An architectural style where components communicate primarily by producing and consuming events through an event broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ), rather than calling each other directly via synchronous request/response.

[Order Service] --publishes--> "OrderPlaced" event --> [Event Broker]
                                                              |
                          +-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
                          |                                   |                                   |
                   [Inventory Service]                [Payment Service]                   [Notification Service]
                   (reserves stock)                    (charges card)                       (sends email)
• Producers don't know or care who (if anyone) consumes their events - full decoupling.
• Contrast with a request-driven architecture, where a service directly calls another service and waits for its response.

expert.content:
The Real Tradeoff: Decoupling vs Traceability

Event-driven systems decouple services beautifully, but at the cost of harder-to-follow control flow ("what actually happens when an order is placed?" now requires tracing through multiple independent consumers instead of reading one call stack) - distributed tracing tools (e.g. OpenTelemetry) become essential, not optional, at this scale.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Event-driven vs request-driven — what's the core difference?Event-driven: producers publish events with no knowledge of consumers (async, decoupled). Request-driven: a caller directly invokes another service and waits for a response (sync, coupled)
What's the main cost of event-driven architecture?Harder-to-trace control flow and eventual consistency, requiring investment in distributed tracing and careful event schema design

beginner.content:
What is Client-Server Architecture?

The most foundational distributed architecture: a client requests a service, and a server provides it. Every web application (browser <-> Spring Boot backend) is a client-server system.

• Thin client - most logic/processing happens on the server; the client just renders results (classic server-rendered web apps).
• Thick/fat client - significant logic runs on the client itself (a modern React SPA, or a native desktop app) and it only calls the server for data.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Thin client vs thick client?Thin: most logic on the server, client just renders. Thick: significant logic runs client-side, server mainly serves data

beginner.content:
What is Pipe and Filter?

Processing is broken into a sequence of independent filter stages, each doing one transformation, connected by pipes that pass data from one filter to the next. Unix command pipelines (cat file | grep error | sort | uniq) are the textbook example - and Java's Stream API is essentially this pattern in library form.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How does Java's Stream API relate to Pipe and Filter?Each intermediate operation (filter, map, sorted) is a "filter" stage; the stream itself acts as the "pipe" carrying data between them
What's a real system-level example beyond Java?Unix shell pipelines (cmd1 | cmd2 | cmd3), where each command is a filter and the pipe (|) connects them

beginner.content:
What is Broker Architecture?

A broker component coordinates communication between distributed components - clients never talk to servers directly, they always go through the broker, which handles lookup, routing, and sometimes marshaling of requests/responses.

• Historically implemented by CORBA and Java RMI registries.
• Today the same idea shows up in message brokers (Kafka/RabbitMQ) and API gateways - a central coordinating layer that decouples who's talking to whom.
• Related to, but broader than, the Message Broker pattern (a Broker Architecture is the architectural style; a Message Broker is one specific technology implementing part of it).

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Name a historical and a modern example of Broker ArchitectureHistorical: CORBA/Java RMI registries. Modern: service meshes (Istio) and message brokers (Kafka/RabbitMQ)

beginner.content:
What is Peer-to-Peer Architecture?

In a P2P system, every node (peer) acts as both client and server - there's no central coordinating authority that all requests must pass through, unlike client-server or broker architectures.

• Real examples: BitTorrent (peers both download AND upload file pieces to each other), blockchain networks (every node validates and relays transactions).
• Tradeoff: no single point of failure and can scale organically as more peers join, but coordination/consistency (agreeing on shared state) is much harder without a central authority - blockchain's consensus algorithms exist specifically to solve this.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How does P2P differ from client-server?In P2P every node can act as both client and server with no central authority; client-server has a clear, fixed role split
What's the main challenge P2P systems face?Achieving consistency/consensus on shared state without a central coordinator - which is why blockchain systems need consensus algorithms

cheatNotes: Layered Architecture - horizontal layers, each depends only on the one below
Hexagonal Architecture - core isolated behind ports, adapters plug in technology
Clean/Onion Architecture - dependencies always point inward toward the domain
Microservices - independently deployable services, each owning its own data
Modular Monolith - one deployable unit, strict internal module boundaries
Event-Driven Architecture - components communicate via events, fully decoupled
Pipe and Filter - a sequence of independent transformation stages (Java Streams)
Peer-to-Peer - every node is both client and server, no central authority
